items.text: The mixer hums low and steady and you feel the vibration through the soles of Elias's boots at 3:17 AM. Flour dust is all over the air, catching that harsh fluorescent light like it's suspended snow. He wipes his hands on the apron, fabric gone stiff from dried dough and sweat. He moves to the front counter to check the lock. Its a ritual really born of paranoia not necessity. There sat the book, The History of Salt. Hardback, blue spine cracked near the hinge. For six weeks Thursday it just appeared there, always placed right on the glass display case next to the unsold cinnamon rolls. No library stamp to say its from the municipal system, but its not a branch. Elias picks it up. The cover feels cold. He opens it, expecting blank pages or maybe a forgotten bookmark or something. Instead this folded square of lined notebook paper slipped out, landed on the counter with a soft tap. He unfolds it, the handwriting is jagged, pressed hard into the fibre. It says, you knead with left hand dominant, stop favoring right, it ruins the tension. Elias just stares at the words and the mixer ticks over to next cycle. He looks at his own hands, knuckles red, dusted white. He closes the book and puts it back on the glass, lines the spine up with the edge exactly. Then he turns off the overhead light above the display and leaves the book in shadow.

Industrial mixer droned its steady hum vibrating through the boots of Elias. Flour hung in the air catching the light of the fluorescents. It was 3:17 AM. The loaves of sourdough sat on the wooden boards still with their crusts soft and pale. It was before the final bake. He wiped his hands on the apron which was stiff with dried dough and sweat. He moved to the front counter to check the lock. A ritual more born of paranoia than necessity. There sat The History of Salt. Hardback, the blue spine cracked near the hinge. Every Thursday for six weeks it would appear, placed on the glass display case next to the unsold cinnamon rolls. No library stamp. Not a branch of the municipal system. He picked the book up and opened it, expecting blank pages or a forgotten bookmark. But instead, it was a folded square of lined notebook paper that slipped out and landed on the counter with a soft tap. He unfolded it. The handwriting was jagged and pressed hard. "You knead with your left hand dominant. Stop favoring the right. It ruins the tension." He stared at it. The mixer ticked to the next cycle. He looked at his own hands, red-knuckled and dusted white. He closed the book. Placed it back on the glass, aligning the spine perfectly with the edge. Then he turned off the overhead light above the display. Leaving the book in shadow.

That sourdough was on its second rise when I found it. It happens every Thursday. Right on top of the flour bin and always that copy of The Count of Monte Cristo with the Richmond Public Library stamp. I don't know how they get past the squeaky screen door without me hearing but I think my brain's mostly yeast and caffeine by 3 AM anyway. The Count's the first novel I owned which is kind of funny considering all the other books I have. So far no one's picked up the bag, so maybe it'll stay there. Or maybe not. But tonight a scrap of yellow legal paper was poking out of the top like a bookmark. And what did it say. Page 142. Please. I think they're watching the drop box now. The note was written in spiky frantic handwriting and I wiped my hands on my apron leaving ghostly white smudges on the dark cloth. A cold draft went through the kitchen smelling of wet asphalt and rain coming in. I looked toward the darkened front windows but I could only see my own tired reflection staring back. I didn't open the book. Instead I tucked the note back between the pages and slid the novel into a brown pastry bag and folded the top down twice to seal it up.

So it turns out every Thursday at 2:17, Mara had this book left on the bakery back step. Same book both times before. Its a field guide to north American moths, county library sticker ghost pale on the spine. A little flour is worked into the jacket as if the book had been helping, so she had returned it twice and the librarians just smiled too politely and by the third week she had kept it beside her rye starter and said nothing. 

Tonight. Rain ticked against the alley door, ovens breathed, she was working on her croissants, pressing the butter into the dough, palms against the dough. Latch clicks, that tiny guilty click. No one there. Just the book dry as a bone, on the wet concrete. 

She wiped her hands on her apron, opened the book. A slip of paper between the luna moth entry and the promethea entry, folded once. It says your window is the only light on this street. I read here until the first bus. Im sorry about the crumbs. 

Mara looks at the alley, dented milk crates, steam rising off the drains, the city feels enormous for a second and then not. Tors a corner off an order pad, writes: cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05. Then puts the note inside, places it on the warm windowsill, unlocks the back door.

At 2:17 every Thursday morning Mara found the library book on the bakery back step. Always the same one, "A Field Guide to North American Moths" the county library sticker was ghost pale on the spine. It had flour worked into the jacket, as if the book had been helping. She returned it twice and the librarians smiled too politely. By the third week she just kept it beside the rye starter and said nothing.

Tonight rain ticked against the alley door and the ovens breathed. Mara was shaping croissants, pressing butter into dough, when the latch gave its tiny, guilty click. No one there, just the book lying dry as a bone on the wet concrete. She wiped her hands on her apron and opened it. Between the Luna Moth and Promethea there was a slip of paper folded once. It said "your window is the only light on this street. I read here until the first bus. I'm sorry about the crumbs."

Mara looked out at the alley, the dented milk crates, steam rising off the drains. The city felt enormous for a second and then not. She tore a corner off an order pad and wrote that cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05. Then she put the note in the book, set it on the warm windowsill and unlocked the back door.

Marguerite got the book off the steel table. It was in that shelf by the back door where the bread peels hang. It's this field guide to coastal birds. There's a library stamp in the cover. Harbor Street branch and a due date in March. The mail slot had been nailed shut a while but the delivery hatch there which the flour man uses never latches properly. Eleven Thursdays she was looking. She'd ask the day staff, checked the hatch for scratches, and once she stayed past 4pm with her coat on just to check. And it never got here. It was somewhere between two and four. It was just not there. She was always at the ovens, back to the door, it never arrived. Now there's a receipt from Pells, grocery. Someone put a receipt on oyster catchers page, folded it in there. The writing is quite blotchy. The ink had gone blotchy where someone pressed too hard.

I keep meaning to take this back to the library. Then I pass your door and there's the smell of bread and I put it down instead. I can stop if you want. She smelled of salt she thought, whoever it was. Because the pages smelled of salt. And she took a pencil off her apron. Wrote on the back of the receipt. Bring it Thursday, I'll have a roll. And tucked it in the page again. Put the book on the hatch ledge. Put a warm roll in a paper bag beside the book.

Marguerite found the book on the steel table by the back door, under the bench where the bread peels hang, A Field Guide to Coastal Birds. Inside the cover it has that Harbor Street branch stamp and the due date was March. The mail slot in that door got nailed shut years ago but the delivery hatch next to it, the one the flour man uses, never latched properly. For eleven Thursdays, she'd asked day staff and looked for scratches on the hatch, even once stayed till after four wearing her coat. Nothing. But the book showed up between two and four and she was always at the ovens, back to the door, when it did.

Tonight a receipt from Pell's grocery was folded into the oystercatcher page. Where it got pressed hard, the ink went blotchy.

I keep meaning to take this back to the library. Then I pass your door and there's the smell of bread and I put it down instead. I can stop if you want.

She thought, of the salt smell. Whoever it was she thought they smelled of salt, because the pages did smell of salt. Marguerite pulled out her pencil and wrote on the back of the receipt. Bring it Thursday, I'll have a roll. She tucked it in at oystercatchers, set the book on the hatch ledge, and put a warm roll in a paper bag next to it.

So 3:40 a.m. the second batch of rye was proofing. And Marisol sees the book again. On the flour bin by the back door. It's stamped Eastgate Branch and due three weeks ago. Fourth Thursday in a row with the same book, A Field Guide to Night Birds. She's been putting it in the drop box on the way home every time. And it comes back anyway like it's haunted. She wipes her hands on the apron. Opens it. There's an index card folded on the barn owls page. It says leave the vent fan on, she's walking her mother's dog because her mother can't do it anymore. She keeps forgetting to return the book, maybe she's not wanting to. Signed R. She read it twice and then over. The fan's pushing warm air out the door into the alley. On the backside she's writing rye comes out at 4:15. With the grease pencil from the tray. Tearing a heel from yesterday's loaf, wrapping it up in wax paper, setting it on top of the book, propping the door open an inch.

The second batch of rye was proofing and Marisol found it again at 3:40am. Library book sat on the flour bin by the back door, plastic jacket cold from the alley. Fourth Thursday in a row. Same book, A Field Guide to Night Birds, stamped Eastgate Branch, due three weeks ago. She carried it to the drop box every time she went home. Every Thursday it came back, as if the building itself had borrowed it. She wiped her hands on her apron and opened it. A folded index card came out from the page on barn owls. You leave the vent fan on, the alley smells like bread until five, she walks her mother's dog now because her mother can't anymore, she keeps forgetting to return it, maybe she keeps not wanting to. Signed R. Read it twice while the oven timer counted down. Outside the fan was humming pushing warm air into the dark. She turned the card over and wrote rye's out at 4:15 with the grease pencil she used for marking trays. Tore a heel from yesterday's loaf, wrapped it in wax paper, put the book on top of it, propped the back door open about an inch.

Thursdays, the book shows up. Not on the counter, mind you, but wedged behind the flour bins by the back door. Whoever leaves it clearly knows exactly where I won't trip over it. It's always the same book. A Field Guide to North American Moths. Elmwood branch. Due date stamped so long ago the ink's gone violet. I've never seen anyone drop it off. I'm elbow deep in rye dough by two and honestly at that hour I wouldn't even notice a marching band. The first few weeks I just set it on the shelf by the register, and by Friday morning it was gone. Thursday it was back again. Fine, people are strange. I'm a guy who talks to his sourdough starter so I'm not judging. Tonight there was a note tucked at page 114, on the luna moths. It says: They only live a week. They don't even eat. I keep thinking that's a waste of a beautiful thing. Do you ever get to see the bread before it's gone. No signature, just pencil, pressed hard. I read it twice, then a third time while the ovens ticked. Then I pulled the first loaf of the night out, still crackling, wrapped it in brown paper and set it behind the flour bins.
